title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 18 Sep 2026]
    Title:AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.

report.summary: AutoViewMem reorganizes conversational long-term memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views at write time, boosting LLM agent retrieval and personalization without complex retrieval-time pipelines.
report.background: LLM agents increasingly need persistent memory to stay consistent and personalized across long conversations, but most systems store everything in one flat vector space using fixed chunk sizes or static schemas. That works poorly when a single memory mixes heterogeneous content: user preferences, factual events, hard constraints, and time-sensitive updates. Mixing these creates semantic interference, so standard top-K similarity search pulls noisy or poorly ranked evidence. Recent work has tried routing, iterative retrieval, and graph structures to compensate, but these add latency and complexity. AutoViewMem instead shifts the work to write time: it discovers natural semantic categories from interaction traces, keeps only complementary, low-overlap views, and extracts provenance-grounded memories into them. This reflects a broader industry trend toward representation-first memory design, where better structure beats heavier retrieval machinery.
key_points: The core idea is to disentangle memory before indexing, not during retrieval. AutoViewMem learns which semantic views exist in a user's history, then writes each extracted memory into the right view, so a simple top-K search returns focused evidence.

Views are self-configuring and complementary. The system discovers candidate views from real interaction traces and selects a compact set with low overlap, avoiding both over-fragmentation and the semantic collisions of a single mixed store.

Each memory is provenance-grounded and structured at write time. Because preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates land in distinct views, later updates and contradictions are easier to consolidate and retrieve correctly.
Offline consolidation improves compactness and consistency. Periodic merging reduces redundancy and drift, helping long-horizon agents stay coherent without inflating the memory store.
Experiments on LoCoMo and PersonaMem with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B show gains over strong memory baselines in long-horizon QA and personalization, while preserving a simple inference pipeline.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AutoViewMem points to a practical alternative to ever-more-complex retrieval stacks: better memory representation at write time may deliver more value than routing, re-ranking, or multi-hop retrieval at query time. Developers building assistants, copilots, and companion agents can adopt the pattern without rewriting their serving path—keep straightforward vector search, but structure writes into orthogonal views. That lowers latency and cost while improving answer quality. Regular users benefit indirectly through assistants that remember preferences without confusing them with stale events or temporary constraints, and that stay personalized across weeks or months. The main caution is that learned views must be evaluated for privacy leakage and consolidation errors, since misclassified memories could persist silently.
report.tools: Related open-source projects worth watching: Mem0 and Zep for production memory APIs, Letta (formerly MemGPT) for agent memory loops, LangMem and LlamaIndex memory modules for write-time extraction patterns, and Cognee or Graphiti for structured memory graphs. The LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks are useful for reproducing long-horizon memory evaluations. Also follow retrieval frameworks such as HippoRAG for comparison against representation-first approaches.
